en: Taal Volcano is one of the lowest active volcanoes in the world, with its highest peak standing just 311 meters above sea level.
The small island province of Camiguin has more volcanoes, totaling seven, than it has official municipalities, which number only five.
The Puerto Princesa Subterranean River features an 8.2-kilometer underground waterway that flows directly out of the cave and into the sea.
Crater Lake in Mount Pinatubo is the largest lake in the Philippines formed by a single, massive volcanic eruption in 1991.
The critically endangered Philippine Eagle, the national bird, is found exclusively in the wild mountain forests of the island of Mindanao.
The Galathea Depth in the Philippine Trench is the deepest point in the Philippine Sea, plunging to an incredible 10,540 meters.
The Sierra Madre mountain range stretches over 540 kilometers along the eastern coast of Luzon, making it the longest in the country.
The Philippines is the second-largest global producer of nickel, a highly valuable metal used to manufacture stainless steel and batteries.
The famous Chocolate Hills in Bohol consist of over 1,200 symmetrical, cone-shaped mounds that turn brown during the dry summer season.
The Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park in the Sulu Sea protects a massive coral atoll containing over 600 fish and 360 coral species.
In 2016, advanced mapping technology updated the official count of Philippine islands from 7,107 to the currently recognized 7,641 islands.
The Banaue Rice Terraces in Ifugao were carved into the steep mountains by indigenous ancestors over 2,000 years ago using hand tools.
